nameStory: The Atlantic croaker gets its name from the distinctive croaking sounds it makes, especially when caught or handled. Like other members of the drum family, it produces these grunting, croaking noises using special muscles that vibrate against its swim bladder, creating an underwater chorus that sounds remarkably like a frog pond.
description: The Atlantic croaker is a silvery, medium-sized fish with a slightly compressed body and a distinctive downward-pointing mouth. These coastal fish typically grow to about 12-16 inches long and have a brassy or golden sheen along their sides. They're members of the drum family, known for their ability to make sounds, and are closely related to red drum and weakfish. In New England waters, they're uncommon visitors that occasionally show up in our southern coastal areas.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Moderately deep, laterally compressed body that feels firm and muscular when handled, with a slightly arched back

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, inferior mouth positioned underneath the snout, designed for bottom feeding - the lower jaw is noticeably shorter than the upper

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Silvery overall with a brassy or golden cast along the sides, often with faint dark diagonal lines or spots that feel smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Sound
idTips.description: Makes distinctive croaking or grunting sounds when handled - you can often hear and feel the vibrations when holding the fish

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins - the first spiny and triangular, the second soft-rayed and longer, with a slightly forked tail fin

habitat: Atlantic croakers prefer shallow coastal waters, estuaries, and bays with sandy or muddy bottoms where they can root for food. In New England, they're most likely found in the warmer southern waters around Cape Cod and the islands during summer months. They favor areas with good tidal flow and often feed in eelgrass beds and near shoreline structures.

seasonality.spring: Rare in New England waters during spring as they begin their northward migration from warmer southern waters.
seasonality.summer: Most likely to be encountered in New England during warm summer months, particularly in southern coastal areas and estuaries.
seasonality.fall: May linger in warmer protected bays and estuaries during early fall before migrating south as water temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having migrated south to warmer coastal areas from the Mid-Atlantic to the Gulf of Mexico.

funFact: Atlantic croakers can actually change the pitch and volume of their croaking sounds like an underwater jazz band - males make louder, more frequent calls during spawning season to attract females, and the whole school can create a chorus so loud it's been known to keep people awake on boats anchored nearby!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with spot croaker (which has a distinctive black spot behind the head) or young weakfish. Remember: croakers have that distinctly underslung mouth and make audible sounds when caught, while weakfish have a more terminal mouth and are usually silent.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Atlantic' croaker, this fish ranges well into the Gulf of Mexico and is actually more common in southern waters. In New England, spotting one is somewhat unusual since we're at the northern edge of their range.
compareHints: Atlantic croaker is the only Micropogonias species in our region, but it's easily distinguished from its drum family cousins by its small, underslung mouth and moderate size. Unlike the much larger black drum or red drum, croakers stay relatively small and have that characteristic bottom-feeder mouth shape. They're more similar to spot croaker, but lack the distinctive black spot behind the gills.
